courses.title: Foundations
courses.subtitle: What psychology is & how it works
courses.description: What psychology is & how it works

cards.heading: A definition
cards.body: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior. 'Behavior' is anything an organism does; 'mental processes' are the internal experiences we infer from it.

cards.heading: Why 'scientific' matters
cards.body: Psychology relies on systematic observation and evidence rather than intuition or common sense. Claims are tested, not just asserted.

cards.heading: Four goals
cards.body: Psychologists aim to describe, explain, predict, and (sometimes) change behavior.

quiz.prompt: Psychology is best defined as the study of…
quiz.explanation: It covers both behavior and mental processes, using scientific methods.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT one of psychology's four goals?
quiz.explanation: The four goals are describe, explain, predict, and change.

quiz.prompt: Relying on 'common sense' instead of evidence is a problem because…
options: Intuitions can be biased and untested
quiz.explanation: Intuition feels convincing but is often biased; science tests claims.

cards.heading: Wilhelm Wundt (1879)
cards.body: Opened the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig, Germany — the moment psychology split from philosophy into its own science.

cards.heading: Structuralism
cards.body: Edward Titchener used introspection to break conscious experience into basic 'elements' of sensation and feeling.

cards.heading: Functionalism
cards.body: William James asked what mind is *for* — how consciousness helps us adapt and survive, inspired by Darwin.

quiz.prompt: Who founded the first psychology lab in 1879?
quiz.explanation: Wundt's Leipzig lab marks the birth of psychology as a science.

quiz.prompt: Introspection was the main method of…
quiz.explanation: Structuralists used introspection to find the elements of experience.

quiz.prompt: Functionalism focused on…
quiz.explanation: James asked what mind is for — how it helps us adapt.

cards.heading: One mind, many lenses
cards.body: Modern psychology explains behavior through complementary perspectives — each a different level of analysis.

cards.heading: The seven lenses
cards.body: Biological, psychodynamic, behavioral, cognitive, humanistic, evolutionary, and sociocultural.

cards.heading: Example: anxiety
cards.body: Biological blames brain chemistry; behavioral sees learned associations; cognitive points to catastrophic thoughts; sociocultural to context. All can be partly true.

quiz.prompt: Explaining behavior with brain chemistry uses the ___ perspective.
quiz.explanation: The biological perspective focuses on brain, genes, and neurochemistry.

quiz.prompt: 'People are driven to grow and self-actualize' fits the ___ perspective.
quiz.explanation: Humanistic psychology emphasizes growth, choice, and potential.

quiz.prompt: Focusing on how thoughts and memory shape behavior is the ___ view.
quiz.explanation: The cognitive perspective studies mental processing.

checkpoint.prompt: Psychology became a distinct science when…
checkpoint.explanation: Wundt's 1879 lab is the standard marker.

checkpoint.prompt: Which pairs a thinker with the RIGHT school?
The four goals of psychology are describe, explain, predict, and…
Which perspective would emphasize unconscious conflict?
checkpoint.explanation: The psychodynamic view stresses unconscious drives and conflict.

checkpoint.prompt: The best reason psychology insists on evidence is that…
options: Intuition is often biased and untested
checkpoint.explanation: Systematic evidence corrects our biased intuitions.

cards.heading: The loop
cards.body: Ask a question → form a testable hypothesis → operationally define your variables → collect data → analyze → revise theory. Then repeat.

cards.heading: Operational definition
cards.body: Spelling out exactly how you'll measure a concept. 'Stress' becomes, say, 'heart rate above 100 bpm during a timed task.'

cards.heading: Falsifiability
cards.body: A good hypothesis must be able to be proven wrong. If no evidence could ever contradict it, it isn't scientific.

quiz.prompt: An operational definition…
options: Specifies exactly how a variable is measured
quiz.explanation: It turns a fuzzy concept into something measurable.

quiz.prompt: A scientific hypothesis must be…
quiz.explanation: It must be capable of being shown false.

quiz.prompt: The scientific method is best described as…
quiz.explanation: It loops: test, revise, retest.

cards.heading: Experiments
cards.body: Manipulate an independent variable (IV) and measure a dependent variable (DV), holding other things constant. Only experiments can show cause and effect.

cards.heading: Control & random assignment
cards.body: A control group provides a baseline. Randomly assigning people to groups spreads out differences so the groups start equivalent.

cards.heading: Correlation ≠ causation
cards.body: Correlational studies measure how variables relate without manipulation. A relationship can't tell you which caused which — or if a third variable did.

quiz.prompt: The variable the experimenter manipulates is the…
quiz.explanation: The IV is manipulated; the DV is measured.

quiz.prompt: Only ___ studies can establish cause and effect.
quiz.explanation: Manipulation + control is what licenses causal claims.

quiz.prompt: Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. This shows…
quiz.explanation: A classic third-variable/confound problem.

cards.heading: Protecting participants
cards.body: Core rules: informed consent, the right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality, and debriefing afterward.

cards.heading: The IRB
cards.body: An ethics board reviews studies before they run to weigh risks against benefits. Deception is allowed only when justified and followed by debriefing.

cards.heading: Why it exists
cards.body: Historical studies that harmed participants led to today's strict codes — ethics is not optional paperwork.

quiz.prompt: Telling participants what they experienced afterward is called…
quiz.explanation: Debriefing happens after the study, especially if deception was used.

quiz.prompt: Which is a core ethical requirement?
quiz.explanation: Consent is foundational.

quiz.prompt: An IRB's job is to…
options: Review studies for ethics before they run
quiz.explanation: It weighs risks vs. benefits in advance.

checkpoint.prompt: You measure reaction time as your ___ variable.
checkpoint.explanation: The measured outcome is the DV.

checkpoint.prompt: Random assignment matters because it…
options: Removes the need for a control group
checkpoint.explanation: It balances unknown differences across groups.

checkpoint.prompt: A correlation of −0.8 means…
checkpoint.explanation: Sign = direction, magnitude = strength; −0.8 is strong and inverse.

checkpoint.prompt: Deception in a study is acceptable only if…
options: It is justified and followed by debriefing

checkpoint.prompt: A testable claim that no evidence could ever contradict is…

cards.heading: Learning by association
cards.body: A neutral stimulus becomes able to trigger a reflex after being paired with something that already triggers it.

cards.heading: The four terms
cards.body: Food (UCS) → salivation (UCR). Pair a bell (neutral) with food; the bell becomes a CS that triggers salivation (CR).

cards.heading: Reflex, not choice
cards.body: Classical conditioning works on automatic, involuntary responses — salivation, fear, nausea — not deliberate actions.

quiz.prompt: Before conditioning, the bell is a…
quiz.explanation: It's neutral until paired with the UCS.

quiz.prompt: Salivation to food (before any learning) is the…
quiz.explanation: It's the unconditioned, automatic response.

quiz.prompt: After conditioning, the bell is the ___ and salivation to it is the ___.
quiz.explanation: The bell becomes the conditioned stimulus; the response is conditioned.

cards.heading: Acquisition & extinction
cards.body: Acquisition is learning the CS–UCS link. Extinction is the fading of the CR when the CS keeps appearing without the UCS.

cards.heading: Spontaneous recovery
cards.body: After extinction and a rest, the CR can briefly reappear — showing the association was suppressed, not erased.

cards.heading: Generalization vs discrimination
cards.body: Generalization: similar stimuli trigger the CR. Discrimination: learning to respond only to the specific CS.

quiz.prompt: The CR fades when the bell rings with no food. This is…
quiz.explanation: Repeated CS-without-UCS produces extinction.

quiz.prompt: A dog fearing all men after one scary man shows…
quiz.explanation: Similar stimuli evoke the response = generalization.

quiz.prompt: Spontaneous recovery suggests the association was…
quiz.explanation: It re-emerges, so it was suppressed.

checkpoint.prompt: Match: UCS is to UCR as CS is to…
checkpoint.explanation: The conditioned stimulus triggers the conditioned response.

checkpoint.prompt: 'Little Albert' learning to fear a white rat is an example of…
checkpoint.explanation: A fear reflex was conditioned to a neutral stimulus.

checkpoint.prompt: Responding to a buzzer but NOT a similar tone is…
checkpoint.explanation: Discrimination = responding only to the specific CS.

checkpoint.prompt: Classical conditioning best explains learning of…
To extinguish a conditioned fear you would…
options: Pair the CS with the UCS more
Present the CS repeatedly without the UCS
checkpoint.explanation: CS without UCS weakens the CR.

cards.heading: Consequences shape behavior
cards.body: Skinner showed behavior is strengthened or weakened by what follows it. Reinforcement increases behavior; punishment decreases it.

cards.heading: Positive vs negative
cards.body: 'Positive' = add something; 'negative' = remove something. It's a math sign, not 'good/bad.'

cards.heading: The 2×2
cards.body: Positive reinforcement: give a treat. Negative reinforcement: stop nagging. Positive punishment: add a fine. Negative punishment: take the phone away.

quiz.prompt: Taking away a teen's phone to reduce rudeness is…
quiz.explanation: Removing something to decrease behavior = negative punishment.

quiz.prompt: 'Negative reinforcement' means…
options: Removing something unpleasant to increase behavior
quiz.explanation: Remove an aversive → behavior increases.

quiz.prompt: Reinforcement always ___ behavior.
quiz.explanation: By definition reinforcement strengthens behavior.

cards.heading: Ratio vs interval
cards.body: Ratio schedules reward after a number of responses; interval schedules reward after time passes. Each can be fixed or variable.

cards.heading: The four schedules
cards.body: Fixed-ratio, variable-ratio, fixed-interval, variable-interval — each produces a distinct pattern of responding.

cards.heading: Why slot machines hook us
cards.body: Variable-ratio schedules (reward after an unpredictable number of responses) produce the highest, most extinction-resistant response rates.

quiz.prompt: A slot machine uses a ___ schedule.
quiz.explanation: Unpredictable payout per pull = variable-ratio.

quiz.prompt: Which schedule is MOST resistant to extinction?
quiz.explanation: Variable-ratio produces the most persistent behavior.

quiz.prompt: A paycheck every two weeks is a ___ schedule.
quiz.explanation: Reward after a set time = fixed-interval.

checkpoint.prompt: Skinner's 'operant' behavior is…
Adding a chore to reduce lying is…
checkpoint.explanation: Adding an aversive to reduce behavior.

checkpoint.prompt: Buckling up to stop the annoying beep is reinforced by…
checkpoint.explanation: Removing the aversive beep strengthens buckling.

checkpoint.prompt: Gambling's grip is best explained by…
Compared with classical conditioning, operant conditioning is about…

cards.heading: We learn by watching
cards.body: Bandura showed children imitate aggression they see modeled by adults — learning without any direct reinforcement of their own.

cards.heading: Vicarious reinforcement
cards.body: Seeing a model rewarded (or punished) changes whether we imitate them. We learn from others' consequences.

cards.heading: Four steps
cards.body: Attention → retention → reproduction → motivation. You must notice, remember, be able to do it, and want to.

quiz.prompt: The Bobo doll study demonstrated…
quiz.explanation: Children imitated modeled aggression.

quiz.prompt: Copying a model because you saw them rewarded is…
quiz.explanation: Learning from others' consequences.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT one of Bandura's four steps?
quiz.explanation: The four are attention, retention, reproduction, motivation.

checkpoint.prompt: Observational learning shows that reinforcement…
checkpoint.explanation: We can learn from others' outcomes.

checkpoint.prompt: A child copies a sibling praised for sharing. This is…
checkpoint.explanation: Imitation driven by an observed reward.

checkpoint.prompt: Bandura's approach is often called…
checkpoint.explanation: It blends learning with cognition and social context.

checkpoint.prompt: You can 'know' a skill from watching but not perform it if you lack…
Observational learning differs from operant conditioning because…
options: The learner need not act to learn
checkpoint.explanation: Learning can occur before any behavior is performed.

cards.heading: The multi-store model
cards.body: Information flows through sensory memory → short-term memory → long-term memory. Attention and rehearsal move it along.

cards.heading: Capacity & duration
cards.body: Sensory memory: huge but under a second. Short-term: about 7±2 items for ~15–30 seconds. Long-term: effectively unlimited and lasting.

cards.heading: Chunking
cards.body: Grouping items (like a phone number into blocks) beats short-term memory's small capacity by packing more into each 'slot.'

quiz.prompt: Short-term memory holds roughly…
quiz.explanation: Miller's 'magical number seven, plus or minus two.'

quiz.prompt: Grouping digits to remember them is…
quiz.explanation: Chunking increases effective capacity.

quiz.prompt: The correct flow is…
quiz.explanation: Sensory, then short-term, then long-term.

cards.heading: Three stages
cards.body: Encoding gets information in, storage keeps it, retrieval gets it back out. A 'memory problem' can fail at any stage.

cards.heading: Elaborative rehearsal
cards.body: Linking new material to what you already know (meaning) beats mere repetition for building durable long-term memories.

cards.heading: Retrieval cues
cards.body: Memory improves when the context or mood at recall matches the one at learning — context- and state-dependent memory.

quiz.prompt: Connecting new facts to existing knowledge is…
quiz.explanation: Elaboration creates richer, more durable memories.

quiz.prompt: Forgetting where a memory never formed properly is a failure of…
quiz.explanation: If it never got in, encoding failed.

quiz.prompt: Recalling better in the room you studied in shows…
quiz.explanation: External context acts as a retrieval cue.

checkpoint.prompt: The three memory processes are encoding, storage, and…
Sensory memory is best described as…
For a lasting memory of a concept, best to use…
Studying while slightly caffeinated and recalling best while caffeinated is…
checkpoint.explanation: Internal state as a retrieval cue.

checkpoint.prompt: 'Tip-of-the-tongue' is mainly a failure of…
checkpoint.explanation: The memory exists but can't be accessed — retrieval.

cards.heading: Memory is reconstructive
cards.body: We don't replay recordings — we rebuild memories each time, filling gaps with expectations. That makes memory editable.

cards.heading: The misinformation effect
cards.body: Loftus showed that misleading questions after an event can alter what people 'remember' seeing.

cards.heading: The car crash study
cards.body: Asking how fast cars were going when they 'smashed' (vs 'hit') led to higher speed estimates and more false memories of broken glass.

quiz.prompt: Loftus's work shows memory is…
quiz.explanation: We rebuild memories, so they can be altered.

quiz.prompt: Misleading post-event questions cause the…
quiz.explanation: Later information reshapes the memory.

quiz.prompt: In the crash study, the verb 'smashed' led people to…
options: Recall higher speeds and false glass
quiz.explanation: Wording biased their reconstructed memory.

checkpoint.prompt: The main lesson of Loftus's research is that…
options: Memory can be distorted by later information

checkpoint.prompt: A false memory is…
options: A confidently held memory of something that didn't happen
checkpoint.explanation: It feels real but is inaccurate.

checkpoint.prompt: Reconstructive memory means we fill gaps with…
checkpoint.explanation: Prior knowledge and expectations fill in gaps.

checkpoint.prompt: This research strongly affects the reliability of…
High confidence in a memory means it is…
checkpoint.explanation: Confidence and accuracy are only loosely linked.

courses.title: Development
courses.subtitle: How we grow across a lifetime
courses.description: How we grow across a lifetime

cards.heading: Building blocks of thought
cards.body: A schema is a mental framework for organizing information. Children build and revise schemas as they explore.

cards.heading: Assimilation vs accommodation
cards.body: Assimilation fits new experiences into existing schemas; accommodation changes the schema to fit reality.

cards.heading: The 'doggy' example
cards.body: A toddler calls every four-legged animal 'doggy' (assimilation), then learns cats are different and updates the schema (accommodation).

quiz.prompt: A mental framework for organizing knowledge is a…
quiz.explanation: Schemas organize thinking.

quiz.prompt: Changing a schema to fit new information is…
quiz.explanation: Accommodation updates the schema.

quiz.prompt: Calling a cat a 'dog' fits new info into an old schema — this is…
quiz.explanation: The experience is forced into the existing schema.

cards.heading: Sensorimotor (0–2)
cards.body: Infants learn through senses and action; the key milestone is object permanence — knowing things exist when out of sight.

cards.heading: Preoperational (2–7)
cards.body: Symbolic thought and language bloom, but children are egocentric and fail conservation (that quantity stays the same despite shape changes).

cards.heading: Concrete & formal
cards.body: Concrete operational (7–11): logical about concrete things, master conservation. Formal operational (12+): abstract and hypothetical reasoning.

quiz.prompt: Object permanence develops in the ___ stage.
quiz.explanation: It's the hallmark of the sensorimotor stage.

quiz.prompt: Failing conservation and being egocentric marks the ___ stage.
quiz.explanation: Preoperational children can't yet conserve.

quiz.prompt: Abstract, hypothetical reasoning appears in the ___ stage.
quiz.explanation: Formal operational thought handles abstraction.

checkpoint.prompt: Piaget believed children think…
checkpoint.explanation: Each stage is a different kind of thinking.

checkpoint.prompt: A child knows a hidden toy still exists. They have…
Conservation is typically mastered in the ___ stage.
Egocentrism in Piaget means…
checkpoint.explanation: It's a cognitive limitation, not a personality flaw.

checkpoint.prompt: Updating a schema after surprising evidence is…

cards.heading: The bond that shapes us
cards.body: Attachment is the deep emotional bond between infant and caregiver. Bowlby argued it is a survival system with lifelong effects.

cards.heading: The Strange Situation
cards.body: Ainsworth watched how babies reacted to separation and reunion with a caregiver to classify attachment styles.

cards.heading: Three classic styles
cards.body: Secure (distressed at leaving, comforted at return), insecure-avoidant (indifferent), and insecure-resistant/ambivalent (distressed and hard to soothe).

quiz.prompt: Ainsworth's method for measuring attachment is the…
quiz.explanation: It observes separation and reunion.

quiz.prompt: A baby who is comforted quickly on reunion is likely…
quiz.explanation: Secure infants use the caregiver as a safe base.

quiz.prompt: Attachment theory was pioneered by…
quiz.explanation: Bowlby framed attachment as an evolved system; Ainsworth measured it.

checkpoint.prompt: Attachment is best described as…
options: An emotional bond with survival value
checkpoint.explanation: Bowlby saw it as an evolved bonding system.

checkpoint.prompt: In the Strange Situation, the key moments are…
checkpoint.explanation: Reactions to leaving and returning classify style.

checkpoint.prompt: An infant indifferent to a caregiver leaving and returning is likely…
A 'safe base' allows a securely attached child to…
Attachment research suggests early bonds…
checkpoint.explanation: Early attachment can influence later relating.

cards.heading: The power of the group
cards.body: Conformity is adjusting behavior or opinion to match a group. Asch showed people will deny obvious facts to fit in.

cards.heading: The line study
cards.body: Asked to match line lengths, many participants gave answers they could see were wrong — just because confederates did.

cards.heading: Two reasons we conform
cards.body: Normative influence (to be liked/accepted) and informational influence (to be right when unsure).

quiz.prompt: Asch's line study measured…
quiz.explanation: Matching a group's obviously wrong answer.

quiz.prompt: Conforming to be accepted by the group is ___ influence.
quiz.explanation: Normative influence = wanting to fit in.

quiz.prompt: Conforming because you assume the group knows better is ___ influence.
quiz.explanation: Informational influence = seeking to be correct.

cards.heading: Obedience to authority
cards.body: Milgram tested how far ordinary people would go when an authority figure told them to harm another person.

cards.heading: The shock study
cards.body: A majority of participants (about two-thirds) continued to the maximum 'shock' level when urged by the experimenter.

cards.heading: The lesson
cards.body: Situational pressure and legitimate-seeming authority — not evil personalities — drove obedience. Situations shape behavior powerfully.

quiz.prompt: Milgram studied…
quiz.explanation: Following an authority's harmful orders.

quiz.prompt: Roughly what fraction went to the maximum shock?
quiz.explanation: About 65% obeyed to the end.

quiz.prompt: Milgram's main conclusion was that behavior is powerfully shaped by…
quiz.explanation: Situational forces, not just character.

checkpoint.prompt: Denying an obvious perceptual fact to match a group is…
Normative influence is driven by the need to…
Milgram's participants mostly obeyed because of…
Obedience differs from conformity in that obedience involves…
options: A direct order from an authority

checkpoint.prompt: A key ethical concern in Milgram's study was…

cards.heading: The discomfort of contradiction
cards.body: Festinger's cognitive dissonance is the tension we feel when our attitudes and actions clash. We're motivated to reduce it.

cards.heading: The $1 vs $20 study
cards.body: People paid just $1 to say a boring task was fun later rated it as MORE fun — they changed their attitude to justify a poorly-paid lie.

cards.heading: How we resolve it
cards.body: We reduce dissonance by changing the attitude, changing the behavior, or adding a justification.

quiz.prompt: Cognitive dissonance is the tension between…
quiz.explanation: Inconsistency between beliefs and actions.

quiz.prompt: In the classic study, who liked the boring task MORE?
quiz.explanation: Small payment gave weak justification, so they changed the attitude.

quiz.prompt: One way to reduce dissonance is to…
options: Change your attitude to match your action
quiz.explanation: Aligning attitude with behavior resolves it.

checkpoint.prompt: Cognitive dissonance theory was proposed by…
Paying someone MORE to lie tends to produce ___ attitude change.
checkpoint.explanation: Big payment justifies the lie, so less attitude change.

checkpoint.prompt: Dissonance is best described as a state of…
'I smoke but smoking is bad' can be eased by…
Dissonance research shows behavior can change…

courses.title: Personality
courses.subtitle: What makes each of us us
courses.description: What makes each of us us

cards.heading: A mind in three parts
cards.body: Freud proposed the id (unconscious drives, 'I want it now'), the superego (morals and ideals), and the ego (the realistic mediator).

cards.heading: The pleasure vs reality principle
cards.body: The id runs on the pleasure principle; the ego on the reality principle, delaying gratification to keep us functioning.

cards.heading: Mostly hidden
cards.body: Freud pictured the mind as an iceberg — most mental life is unconscious, influencing us without our awareness.

quiz.prompt: The impulsive, pleasure-seeking part is the…
quiz.explanation: The id demands immediate gratification.

quiz.prompt: The realistic mediator between drives and morals is the…
quiz.explanation: The ego balances id and superego with reality.

quiz.prompt: The superego represents our…
quiz.explanation: The superego is conscience and ideals.

cards.heading: Protecting the ego
cards.body: Defense mechanisms are unconscious strategies that reduce anxiety by distorting reality.

cards.heading: Common ones
cards.body: Repression (push away), denial (refuse to accept), projection (attribute your feelings to others), displacement (redirect onto a safer target).

cards.heading: Sublimation
cards.body: Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially valued activity — like turning aggression into competitive sport — is the 'healthiest' defense.

quiz.prompt: Accusing others of the hostility you feel is…
quiz.explanation: Projection attributes your feelings to others.

quiz.prompt: Taking out work anger on your family is…
quiz.explanation: Displacement redirects onto a safer target.

quiz.prompt: Channeling impulses into valued work or art is…
quiz.explanation: Sublimation transforms impulses constructively.

checkpoint.prompt: Freud's iceberg metaphor stresses the power of the…
checkpoint.explanation: Most of the mind is hidden.

checkpoint.prompt: A toddler-like tantrum in an adult under stress is…
The ego operates on the ___ principle.
Defense mechanisms mainly work to…
checkpoint.explanation: They protect the ego from anxiety.

checkpoint.prompt: A major modern criticism of Freud's theory is that it is…

cards.heading: A ladder of needs
cards.body: Maslow arranged needs in a pyramid: we generally satisfy lower needs before pursuing higher ones.

cards.heading: The five levels
cards.body: Physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization (reaching your full potential).

cards.heading: Rogers' humanism
cards.body: Carl Rogers stressed unconditional positive regard and congruence between our real self and ideal self as keys to growth.

quiz.prompt: The top of Maslow's pyramid is…
quiz.explanation: Reaching full potential sits at the top.

quiz.prompt: Food, water, and sleep are ___ needs.
quiz.explanation: The base of the pyramid.

quiz.prompt: Rogers' 'unconditional positive regard' means…
quiz.explanation: Accepting a person fully, regardless of behavior.

cards.heading: Traits, measured
cards.body: Modern trait theory describes personality along five broad dimensions, each a spectrum.

cards.heading: OCEAN
cards.body: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism — the most empirically supported model of personality.

cards.heading: Why it matters
cards.body: Unlike Freud's ideas, the Big Five is measurable, reliable, and predictive — a cornerstone of scientific personality psychology.

quiz.prompt: The Big Five acronym OCEAN's 'N' stands for…
quiz.explanation: Neuroticism = emotional instability vs stability.

quiz.prompt: Being organized and dependable reflects high…
quiz.explanation: Conscientiousness covers self-discipline and order.

quiz.prompt: The Big Five is favored by scientists because it is…
quiz.explanation: It's empirically grounded and reliable.

checkpoint.prompt: Humanistic psychology emphasizes…
Which need must generally be met before esteem needs?
checkpoint.explanation: Belonging comes before esteem in the pyramid.

checkpoint.prompt: The five OCEAN traits include all EXCEPT…
checkpoint.explanation: Intelligence is not one of the Big Five.
